read.sections.0.text.note: Mount Meru = เขาพระสุเมรุ; Churning of the Ocean of Milk = การกวนเกษียรสมุทร (standard Thai names). moat = คูน้ำ.
read.sections.0.text.source:
A great building can show who had the resources to order it. A monument is a large structure that can honour or communicate something. It brings together labour, materials, knowledge and authority. Its layout may also express ideas about religion and the order of the world. So studying a monument means studying people and institutions, not only height or beauty.

Angkor Wat was built in the twelfth century under the Khmer king Suryavarman II. It was dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu. Patronage means support for making or caring for art or buildings. The king's patronage of a great temple connected him with sacred authority. Sacred means having religious importance. The project also needed organised labour and specialist knowledge. The patron's role helps explain the project. But it does not name every worker, or tell us what everyone thought about the ruler.

Its five central towers stand for Mount Meru, a sacred mountain in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. Galleries and a moat (a wide channel of water around it) help make the building a picture of a universe. Stone reliefs tell Hindu stories, including the Churning of the Ocean of Milk. Buildings and images expressed ideas together. The photographs show the temple from a distance. Research supplies meanings that a view alone cannot show.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A great building can show who had enough resources to order it built. A monument is a large structure that may honour or communicate something. Monuments bring together labour, materials, knowledge and power. A monument's layout may also show ideas about religion and the order of the world. So studying a monument means studying people and institutions, not just height or beauty.

Angkor Wat was built in the 12th century in the reign of King Suryavarman II, a Khmer king, and dedicated to Vishnu, a Hindu god. Patronage means supporting the making or care of art or buildings. A king's patronage of a great temple connected him with sacred power. Sacred means religiously important. The work also needed systematically organised labour and specialist knowledge. The patron's role helps explain the work, but doesn't give every worker's name or tell what everyone thought of the ruler.

The five central towers symbolise Mount Meru, the sacred mountain in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. Galleries and a moat (a wide surrounding channel of water) help make the building a model of the universe. Reliefs in the stone tell Hindu stories, including the churning of the ocean of milk. Building and images express ideas together. The photograph shows the temple from a distance; research gives meanings that looking alone cannot show.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: "the 1100s" = ช่วงปี 1100 ถึง 1199, as in KEY_TERMS.
read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A big building can show who had the money and power to order it. A monument is a large building with a meaning. It needs workers, materials, skill and power. Its shape can also show ideas about religion and the world.

Angkor Wat was built in the 1100s. The Khmer king Suryavarman II had it made. It was made for the Hindu god Vishnu. Patronage means paying for or supporting a building. The king's patronage linked him with sacred power. Sacred means holy. Many workers and experts built it. But we do not know all their names. We also do not know what everyone thought of the king.

Its five middle towers stand for Mount Meru. This is a holy mountain in Hindu and Buddhist stories. Walkways and a moat help the temple show a whole universe. A moat is a wide ditch of water around a building. Stone carvings tell Hindu stories. The photos show the temple from far away. Research tells us what a photo cannot.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
A big building can show who had enough money and power to order it built. A monument is a large structure with meaning. It needs workers, materials, skill and power. Its form can also show ideas about religion and the world.

Angkor Wat was built in 1100 to 1199. King Suryavarman II, a Khmer king, had it built. The temple was dedicated to Vishnu, a Hindu god. Patronage means paying for or supporting the building of something. The king's patronage linked him with sacred power. Sacred means religiously important. Many workers and specialists built it together, but we don't know all their names. We also don't know what everyone thought of the king.

The five central towers symbolise Mount Meru, a sacred mountain in Hindu and Buddhist stories. Galleries and a moat help the temple show a picture of the whole universe. A moat is a wide channel of water around a building. Carvings in the stone tell Hindu stories. The photograph shows the temple from far away. Research tells what the photograph cannot.

read.sections.1.heading.source: A kingdom and a wider landscape
read.sections.1.heading.back: A kingdom and a wider landscape

read.sections.1.text.note: landscape = ภูมิทัศน์; "shaped by nature and by people" = ถูกปรับแต่งโดยธรรมชาติและโดยผู้คน (หล่อหลอม is an alternative). reservoirs = อ่างเก็บน้ำ (บาราย is the specialist word).
read.sections.1.text.source:
The Khmer kingdom was a state in the past whose centre and rulers changed. Angkor holds the remains of several capitals, one after another, not one building or one unchanging city. Its cultural links reached across Southeast Asia. Khmer builders adapted religious and building ideas linked with the Indian subcontinent, while developing their own local forms. Calling the site Cambodian today should not squeeze these centuries into the modern country's borders. Nor should it suggest that the builders simply copied a foreign model.

Angkor Wat belongs to this wider Angkor landscape. A landscape is an area shaped by nature and by people. UNESCO describes temples, routes, reservoirs, canals and other water structures. The monument stood in a lived-in setting with farming and transport, not alone among empty scenery. Sacred meanings and practical water management can belong to the same landscape. The moat does not need to have only one purpose.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The Khmer kingdom was a past state whose centres and rulers changed over time. Angkor holds the remains of several capitals built one after another, not one building or one city that never changed. Angkor's cultural connections spread across Southeast Asia. Khmer builders adapted religious and building ideas linked with the Indian subcontinent while developing their own local styles. Calling this place Cambodian today shouldn't squeeze those many hundreds of years into a modern country's borders, nor suggest the builders simply copied foreigners.

Angkor Wat is part of this wider Angkor landscape. A landscape is an area shaped by nature and by people. UNESCO describes temples, routes, reservoirs, canals and other water structures. The monument stood in a place where people lived, farmed rice and transported things, not alone among empty scenery. Sacred meaning and practical water management can be part of the same landscape; a moat needn't have only one purpose.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
The Khmer kingdom lasted a long time. Its rulers and its capital changed. Angkor has the remains of several capitals, not just one city. The Khmer had links across Southeast Asia. Their builders used ideas from India. But they made their own local styles. Today Angkor is in Cambodia. But the old kingdom was not the same as the modern country. And its builders did not just copy others.

Angkor Wat is part of a bigger landscape. A landscape is land shaped by nature and by people. It has temples, roads, canals, lakes for storing water and other water works. People lived and farmed there. So the temple did not stand alone in empty land. The moat could be holy and useful at the same time.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
The Khmer kingdom lasted a long time. Its rulers and capitals changed many times. Angkor has the remains of several capitals, not just one city. The Khmer had connections across Southeast Asia. Their builders used ideas from India but also created their own local style. Today Angkor is in Cambodia, but the ancient kingdom was not the same as the modern country, and the builders didn't just copy others.

Angkor Wat is part of a bigger landscape. A landscape is land that nature and people change together. Here there are temples, roads, canals, water-storage lakes and other water structures. People lived and farmed there. So the temple did not stand alone on empty land. A moat can be sacred and useful at the same time.

read.sections.2.text.note: APSARA National Authority = องค์การอัปสราแห่งชาติ.
read.sections.2.text.source:
The temple's use changed. Cambodia's APSARA National Authority describes how it became a Buddhist sacred place. Inscriptions from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries record pilgrims' acts of devotion, including visits by royalty. Some are written in languages other than Khmer. These records show later people actively making the temple meaningful, not simply receiving an unchanging object. This long process should not be reduced to one date when every part changed religion.

Angkor is still living heritage, with communities and religious practice alongside conservation. Conservation means careful, informed care for important places or objects. Caring for Angkor involves both the stones and the people connected with them. The stonework you see today has lasted through use, repair, research and care. A fuller explanation connects the temple's form with royal patronage, a working landscape and changing human meanings over time. A temple's history can go on long after its first patron is gone.
read.sections.2.text.back:
The temple's use changed. Cambodia's APSARA National Authority describes how the temple became a Buddhist sacred place. Inscriptions from the 16th to 18th centuries record pilgrims' acts of devotion, including visits by royalty. Some inscriptions are written in languages other than Khmer. These records show that later people actively gave the temple meaning, rather than just receiving an unchanging object. This long process should not be shrunk to a single day when everything changed religion.

Angkor is also living heritage, with communities and religious practice alongside conservation. Conservation means caring for an important place or object carefully and with knowledge. Caring for Angkor involves both the stones and the people bound up with them. The stonework you see today has been through use, repair, research and care. A fuller explanation connects the temple's form with royal patronage, a landscape in use and meanings people gave that changed over time. A temple's history can continue long after its first patron has gone.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: "from the 1500s to the 1700s" = ช่วงปี 1500 กว่าถึงปี 1700 กว่า, so both numbers stay. Check it reads naturally.
read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Later, the temple's use changed. It became a Buddhist holy place. Words carved in the stone tell of pilgrims who came to pray. Some of these visitors were royal. The words are from the 1500s to the 1700s. Some are in languages other than Khmer. They show that later people gave the temple new meaning. The change did not happen on one single date.

Today Angkor is living heritage. People live nearby and practise their religion there. Others work on conservation. Conservation means taking careful care of old places. The stones we see have lasted because people used, repaired and studied them. A temple's story goes on long after the king who had it made.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Later, the temple's use changed. It became a Buddhist sacred place. Words carved on the stone tell of pilgrims who came to pray. Some visitors were royalty. These texts come from the 1500-somethings to the 1700-somethings. Some are in languages other than Khmer. These texts show that later people gave the temple new meaning. The change did not happen in one day.

Today Angkor is living heritage. People live nearby and practise their religion there. Some work in conservation. Conservation means caring carefully for old places. The stones we see still stand because people use, repair and study them. The temple's story goes on long after the king who had it built has gone.

write.example.source: One part of Angkor Wat is the wide moat around the temple. The reading tells us that Angkor had canals, lakes for storing water and other water works, and that people farmed and travelled there. This links the temple with a working landscape. It was not just a holy building standing alone. The moat could be sacred and useful at the same time. The photos show water, but not the whole system.
write.example.back: One part of Angkor Wat is the wide moat around the temple. The reading tells us that Angkor had canals, water-storage lakes and other water structures, and people farmed rice and travelled there. This connects the temple to a landscape in use. The temple was not just a sacred building standing alone. A moat can be sacred and useful at the same time. The photograph shows water but not the whole system.
